title: Russell Brand prison message denying rape 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says
originalTitle: Russell Brand prison message denying rape 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says
content:
Russell Brand's message to his podcast followers in which he claimed he was innocent of sex offences he has been convicted of was "clearly appalling" and is being urgently investigated, Downing Street has said.

Brand has been convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and is serving a 10-and-half-year sentence. He is currently being held at HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire.

His wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, in which the convicted rapist claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

The Victims' Commissioner for London, Andrea Simon, told Radio 4's Today programme that Brand's claims of innocence will "certainly retraumatise his victims and other survivors of rape who have to hear it".

The prime minister's official spokesman said: "We expect action to be taken if he's found to have broken the rules.

"Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

Responding to the video earlier, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Sky News: "His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it's revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments."

"No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments," he added.

In her Today interview, Simon added: "The victims during the sentencing hearing highlighted how his denials and ongoing media fame over two decades had added to their pain and trauma," she said.

"The fact survivors are still having to hear this now is really problematic and very concerning that we can't do more to protect them from it."

While freedom of expression allows convicted sex offenders such as Brand to profess their innocence, Simon said terms of service of media platforms should regulate "the way in which they get their message out".

She added that prison rules should also be reviewed to "bar those convicted of sending messages to be broadcast" unless permission is granted by the prison governor.

The foreign secretary apologised for having appeared on the former comedian's online show in 2015, when he was Labour leader.

On BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Monday, Miliband said if he'd known about the allegations then, he would not have done the interview.

"I deeply regret doing that interview and all my sympathies are with those victims and we should listen to those victims," he said.

Over the weekend, Brand was moved from HMP Wandsworth in south London to Littlehey prison in Cambridgeshire, a prison that mostly houses sex offenders and has tailored programmes for them.

His wife said on the podcast that she had been speaking to him and he "is OK and is praying".

Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty, told LBC he agreed it was not "a good look" that he'd been moved to a lower security prison.

"I think people want to see him facing the appropriate punishment for what are appalling crimes against women and others and I think the whole episode is shocking," he said.
